chapter.name: Number Play
chapter.blurb: An exploratory chapter of number games and puzzles: rule-based number sequences, supercells in grids, number-line and digit-sum patterns, palindromes, Kaprekar's constant, clock and calendar digit patterns, mental math with a fixed set of numbers, the unsolved Collatz Conjecture, estimation, and turn-based counting games with winning strategies.

concepts.name: Supercells in Number Grids
concepts.description: Identifying a supercell -- a cell whose number is greater than every number in its immediately adjacent cells -- in a 1D row and a 2D grid, and constructing or filling grids to create or avoid supercells.
concepts.idea: A supercell is decided purely by comparing a number with its immediate neighbours, not by its position or its size relative to the whole grid.
concepts.rule: A cell is a supercell only if its number is strictly greater than the number in every one of its adjacent cells (left/right in a row; left/right/top/bottom in a 2D grid). Edge and corner cells have fewer neighbours to beat.
concepts.example: In the row 200, 577, 626, 345, the cell 626 is a supercell because it is greater than both 577 and 345.

concepts.name: Number Line Placement, Digit-Length Counts and Digit Sums
concepts.description: Placing multi-digit numbers correctly on a number line using equal gaps, comparing them, counting how many numbers have a given number of digits, and computing the digit sum of a number.
concepts.idea: The position of a number on a number line, and its digit sum, are two different but useful ways to get a quick sense of a number's size and structure without doing full arithmetic.
concepts.rule: On a number line with equal gaps, values increase steadily in one direction, so an unmarked number can be found by continuing the gap size; the count of numbers with a given number of digits follows the pattern 9, 90, 900, 9000, ..., each ten times the count before it; the digit sum of a number is the sum of its individual digits.

concepts.name: Palindromic Numbers and the Reverse-and-Add Process
concepts.description: Recognising palindromic numbers, constructing them from a given set of digits, and applying the reverse-and-add procedure to reach a palindrome.
concepts.idea: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards; adding a number to its own digit-reversal, repeated as needed, produces a palindrome for every 2-digit starting number tried so far.
concepts.rule: To test if a number is a palindrome, compare its digits from both ends inward. To reverse-and-add: write the digits in reverse order as a new number, add it to the original, and repeat the same reversal-and-addition on the sum until a palindrome appears.
concepts.example: 68 + 86 = 154 (not a palindrome); reverse again: 154 + 451 = 605; continue until a palindrome is reached.

concepts.name: Games and Winning Strategies
concepts.description: Playing turn-based counting games (adding 1-3 to reach 21; adding 1-10 to reach 99) and working out which player has a guaranteed winning strategy and how.
concepts.idea: In a turn-based race-to-a-target game where players add within a fixed range, the winning strategy is to force your opponent to leave you on one of a special sequence of 'safe' numbers, spaced by (1 + the maximum add) apart, counting back from the target.
concepts.rule: If players may add 1 to k on each turn and the target is T, the safe numbers are T, T-(k+1), T-2(k+1), and so on down to a number reachable as a first move; whichever player can always land on a safe number wins.
concepts.example: In the game to 21 where each turn adds 1, 2 or 3, the safe numbers are 21, 17, 13, 9, 5, 1 (steps of 4); the first player wins by starting on 1 and always returning to the next safe number.
